title: Monotone empirical risk minimization
formal: Does every nonempty Boolean concept class \(\mathcal H\subseteq\{0,1\}^X\) of finite VC dimension on a countable domain \(X\) admit a possibly randomized empirical risk minimizer whose expected population error never increases with sample size, under every data distribution? Precisely, for each such \(X,\mathcal H\), require learning rules \(A_n\), \(n\geq1\), that always return an empirical risk minimizer in \(\mathcal H\), and for every distribution \(D\) on \(X\times\{0,1\}\) satisfy \[\mathbb E_{S\sim D^{n+1},R}L_D(A_{n+1}(S,R))\leq\mathbb E_{S\sim D^n,R}L_D(A_n(S,R))\quad(n\geq1).\] The learner may depend on \(\mathcal H\), but not on \(D\).
why: The problem asks whether exact empirical fitting is inherently compatible with the intuition that more independent data should improve expected predictions. It separates the behavior of ERM from general statistical consistency and from monotone wrappers that change the learning rule.
status_note: The ERM existence question is explicit in the checked 2022 paper. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no proof or refutation for the specified countable-domain Boolean finite-VC family. The broader source also asks about other losses and models. Later statements about monotone unrestricted learners, maximum likelihood in well-specified families, or bound-derived risk distributions are not treated as resolutions of this exact ERM claim.

progress.text: The source defines monotonicity of expected risk and poses the broader ERM question.
General monotone-learning constructions are proved, while the existence of monotone ERMs is retained as a separate open question.
The PAC perspective analyzes bound-derived distributions; the checked passage does not establish the exact expected-risk statement of this card.

importance.reason: A basic structural question about empirical risk minimization and finite-sample learning curves, made distinct from known constructions of unrestricted monotone learners.
importance.basis: Individual source review; explicit countable-domain Boolean ERM variant of the broader source direction.

sentences: Expected prediction error can increase when a learner receives an additional independent training example.
This card asks whether every finite-VC Boolean class on a countable domain nevertheless admits a monotone empirical risk minimizer.
The learner may randomize and resolve ties, but must always output an empirically optimal hypothesis from the original class.
Monotonicity is required for every data distribution and every consecutive positive sample size, using actual population error.
A resolution would clarify whether exact empirical fitting can always be reconciled with monotone learning curves.

definitions: The population zero-one loss of \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\) is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). For an ordered sample \(S=((x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_n,y_n))\), its empirical loss is \(\widehat L_S(h)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf1[h(x_i)\ne y_i]\). Each \(A_n\) maps a sample and an independent uniform seed \(R\in[0,1]\) to an element of \(\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal H}\widehat L_S(h)\). This minimum exists because the attainable empirical errors form a nonempty subset of \(\{0,1/n,\ldots,1\}\). Ties may be resolved using the whole ordered sample and the seed; for every fixed sample and test point, the returned label is required to be a measurable function of the seed. With countable \(X\), these conditions make all displayed expectations well defined. No computational or storage bound is imposed. Samples are independent identically distributed draws from \(D\), repetitions are allowed, and the test observation defining population loss is independent of training and of the seed. Labels may be noisy: realizability by \(\mathcal H\) is not assumed. Finite VC dimension means a finite upper bound on the cardinalities of sets \(F\subseteq X\) for which \(\{h|_F:h\in\mathcal H\}=\{0,1\}^F\). The monotonicity compares expectations over samples and learner randomness; it is not a pathwise comparison for each particular sample extension, a statement only after a distribution-dependent threshold, or monotonicity of a generalization bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every class in the stated domain admits such a family of learning rules, or exhibit a class of finite VC dimension on a countable domain and prove that no family of randomized empirical risk minimizers has the displayed property for all \(D,n\). An affirmative proof must retain exact empirical minimization and membership of the output in \(\mathcal H\). For a negative answer, showing nonmonotonicity of one tie-breaking rule does not exclude all eligible ERMs. General monotone learners that need not minimize empirical risk, eventual monotonicity, or decreasing upper bounds on error do not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.text: Viering, Mey and Loog’s original paper asks broadly when learning is monotone and whether it can be made so, emphasizing empirical risk minimization. This card selects the Boolean classification ERM question on countable domains, keeping the broader research direction as provenance instead of presenting it as one unspecified characterization request.

Bousquet, Daniely, Kaplan, Mansour, Moran and Stemmer formulate the remaining ERM question explicitly in their 2022 open-questions section: whether every learnable class admits a monotone empirical risk minimizer. Their general monotone-learning theorem permits rules outside this constraint.

Finite VC dimension controls statistical learning in this setting, but convergence to the best population error need not imply improvement at each consecutive sample size. The quantifier over all distributions includes misspecified or noisy data as well as realizable classification problems.

The 2019 paper provides monotone and nonmonotone examples using the same loss for fitting and evaluation. Such counterexamples show that particular familiar procedures may fail, but do not automatically rule out every permissible ERM rule for a given class.

The 2025 PAC perspective studies distributions constructed from generalization bounds. In its Section 3, a bound-derived expression is used as a distributional model. Monotonicity of that expression alone does not establish the actual expected-risk inequality required here.

Randomization and tie resolution are part of the existence question. The learner can choose among all empirically optimal hypotheses, but cannot replace exact minimization with an arbitrary predictor or select its rule after learning the unknown data distribution.
